# ADR-0073: A run acts as its own scope to Kubernetes, not as its launcher

> **Status:** proposed | **Date:** 2026-11-04

**References:** [RFC-0003:C-HIERARCHY](../rfc/RFC-0003.md#rfc-0003c-hierarchy), [ADR-0067](../adr/ADR-0067.md), [ADR-0068](../adr/ADR-0068.md)

## Context

[ADR-0067](../adr/ADR-0067.md) gave each run controller-minted tokens whose kube_user was the launcher's linked cluster username, so a run's ceiling was the person who launched it. Three problems followed. A launcher who never linked a username got no token at all (GrantError::NoKubeUser), so scheduled runs by unlinked people were silently toolless. A team-owned standing launch had no launcher-shaped principal, so its spend attributed to platform-administrators and its dispatch stamped no usable subject. And a run could do everything its launcher could, in every namespace that launcher could reach, which is far more than any one run needs.

Constraints:

- Kubernetes RBAC is already the authority for every crucible-kueue access check; the SubjectAccessReview carries whatever user and groups the reviewer states, and none of them need to exist as cluster objects.
- The controller knows a run's pod name and its owning scope at token time; it cannot know a person's cluster username without the link machinery this decision removes for runs.
- People's tokens must keep acting as the person: their own RBAC is the ceiling for their MCP clients.


## Decision

A run's token carries its own identity: kube_user `crucible:run:<pod name>` and kube_groups `crucible:runs` plus `crucible:team:<slug>` or `crucible:user:<login>` for its owner. `sub` stays whoever asked for the dispatch, else the owner, so attribution is unchanged.

- The deploy renders ClusterRole `crucible-kueue-caller` — every verb the crucible-kueue access checks can ask, Secret reads narrowed to the profile's pull secrets — bound to Group `crucible:runs` in the `[kueue] shared_namespaces`, an explicit subset of `workload_namespaces` checked at profile load. A team namespace is the same binding to `crucible:team:<slug>`, written by whoever administers that namespace.
- The reviewer refuses a person's token whose user or any group carries the `crucible:` prefix, and a run's token whose user lacks it, as `system:` always was refused: neither kind of token can stand in for the other.
- A run's groups always come from its token; `--kube-authz` describes people's group source only.
- `grant()` records the run's kube_user at dispatch, where the identity is known, and the issuer needs no cluster identity lookup to mint.

Rollout is one Argo sync of both images: the tokens are short-lived, so there is no compatibility branch.


## Consequences

A run can do what its owner's RoleBindings for its scope allow, and no more; a team's runs get exactly what a RoleBinding for `crucible:team:<slug>` grants. Unlinked launchers and team-owned scheduled runs get tokens. A launcher's own broad RBAC no longer reaches into every run they launch. Operators must bind the caller role in each shared namespace before runs can submit there, and the render test that walks every access check keeps a new tool from shipping without its RBAC.
